preamble: Diphthongization of long [iː] to [ai]. In the New High German diphthongization, Middle High German î (written ī in Wiktionary) became ei [aɪ] (snīden > schneiden), alongside û > au [aʊ] and iu > eu [ɔʏ]. The change started in Upper Bavarian as early as the 12th century and reached Moselle Franconian only in the 16th; Alemannic (apart from Swabian) and Ripuarian keep the old long vowel. In many dialects the new ei fell together with the old Middle High German diphthong ei, which was lowered as well; Bavarian monophthongized the old diphthongs instead and kept them apart. The English Great Vowel Shift is not filed here, because Middle English /iː/ of bite went through dated stages, /ei/ (or /əi/) about 1500 and /ɛi/ about 1600, before it reached /aɪ/.
sources: Wikipedia contributors (2026). Early New High German: Phonology. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_New_High_German
